passage:
Early March. Ojas told his father about Jatin, a new friend from the bus who plays drums. Papa laughed at the dinner table: "That long-haired boy? Waste of time." Ojas's phone went into Papa's drawer for a week.
Late March. Ojas said he had extra maths class on Thursdays. In fact he spent the hour in Jatin's garage learning chords, checking the time every few minutes. He hated how easily the story came out now.
First Sunday of April. His mother found him awake at midnight. "Something's weighing on you," she said, and waited. Slowly he told her about the garage and the guitar. She didn't laugh. "Next Thursday I'll come and meet Jatin," she said. "And we'll talk to Papa together."

qa.q: What did Ojas say he was doing on Thursdays?
qa.a: Ojas said he had extra maths class on Thursdays.

qa.q: Why did Ojas start hiding his friendship with Jatin?
qa.a: When he was honest before, Papa laughed at Jatin and took his phone, so Ojas felt the truth wasn't safe to share.

qa.q: What turning point helped Ojas stop lying?
qa.a: His mother waited quietly and listened without laughing, so he felt safe enough to tell the truth and plan an open meeting with Jatin.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had asked about Jatin instead of mocking him?
qa.a: Ojas might have told the truth about the garage from the start, and Papa would know where his son really was.

grounding: A teenage boy hides a friendship after honesty led to ridicule and a confiscated phone, showing that the lie reflects how unsafe the truth felt.

passage:
Yash, you think your Seema Bua doesn't understand your phone business? Listen. When I was sixteen, I had a pen friend in another state, a girl who wrote about her school band. My father opened her first letter and read it aloud at dinner in a silly voice, and my brothers laughed till they cried. After that I had her letters sent to a school friend's house and kept them in my geography book.
I wasn't a bad girl. I just didn't feel safe being honest at home. Years later my father found the stack, read one quietly, and said, "I made you do this, didn't I?" That one sentence mattered more than any scolding. So tell me, what are you afraid I'll do if you tell me?

qa.q: Where did Seema keep the pen friend's letters?
qa.a: Seema kept them in her geography book.

qa.q: Why did young Seema start hiding the letters?
qa.a: Her father read the first letter aloud in a silly voice while her brothers laughed, so she felt honesty at home wasn't safe and wanted to protect the friendship.

qa.q: What choice did Seema's father make when he found the letters, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He read one quietly and admitted, "I made you do this, didn't I?", which mattered to her more than any scolding.

qa.q: How might Seema's father have felt when he found the stack years later?
qa.a: He probably felt regret, realising his mocking had pushed his daughter to hide things, as his quiet question shows.

grounding: An aunt recalls hiding a pen friendship as a teenager because honesty had brought ridicule, showing that the hiding said more about safety than character.
